author: AmandaAskell
text: @RokoMijic I agree. The main thing I'm pointing out is that the principle requires symmetry - it tells you to try to act as if all parties are innocent. Given this, selective applications of it irritate me.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @machinaut I agree it's possible to treat both parties as not guilty. I think my wording was confusing. By "you can't have it both ways" I meant that you can't use the principle to treat the accused as innocent without also treating the accuser as innocent by the same principle.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @RealDarkwing I agree. The principle basically says that until a burden of proof has been met, you must act as if both parties are innocent.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @StefanFSchubert I think there's a broader non-legal version that's something like "don't act as if someone is guilty (e.g. in terms of punishment or social stigma) until a sufficient burden has been met". Which also requires not acting as if accusers are guilty of making false accusations.

author: AmandaAskell
text: If you believe in applying the "presumption of innocence" to non-legal disputes, you will presume that people accused of misconduct are innocent. But you must also presume that the accusers are innocent of making false accusations. You can't have it both ways.

quoted.text: People in ML using “bias” to refer to both ethically-charged biases (“black men are criminals”) & probabilistic biases (“cars are more likely than trucks”) is a fountain of ambiguity. I propose we use “prejudices” for the former & “priors” for the latter & retire the word bias.

author: AmandaAskell

author: AmandaAskell
text: @mormo_music There’s also a methodological concern here. We have two phenomena we’re interested in. We can hypothesize but don’t yet know that one is an instance of the other. I think we should be wary of using terms in a way that presupposes that hypothesis.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @mormo_music I think it would be needed even if the confusion only occurred in cases where we want to express that the encoding of biases is bad or good. Among other things, we want to avoid conflating epistemic and ethical goodness.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @ChrSzegedy Yes, I don’t think these two terms are exhaustive and we might want to have more concepts that currently fall under bias. I’m just not convinced that a catch-all term is doing more benefit than harm here.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @nickcammarata It might be practically rational for someone serving a life sentence to try to lose their desire to be free. But if they tell themselves "life on the outside isn't any better than in here" they're adopting a belief that's practically useful but epistemically unjustified.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @nickcammarata I'm not sure it requires a lot of suffering and the collective upsides seem huge. But to be clear, I think for some people it isn't practically rational to fear death. I just think their practical reasons aren't grounded in insights about the badness of death.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @harrypetolitics In a sense, but I think we secretly hope there's some insight about the badness of death that would make us rational not to fear it. Rather than just the insight "welp, there's nothing I can do it and feeling fear kinda sucks."

author: AmandaAskell
text:
@nickcammarata Fear helps us make rational decisions about risks. It doesn't require feeling fear all the time so I think it's compatible with the benefits you mention.

And if we didn't engage in denial or consolation about death so much, I think we'd have made more progress towards ending it.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @nickcammarata I think it's rational to fear death. I think death is bad and fear causes you to try to prevent it. But if you genuinely can't do anything about it, you would probably be emotionally better off if you try to reduce your fear, including by adopting false beliefs about its badness.

author: AmandaAskell
text: We like to think those who don't fear death are wiser than those who do. That true insight would make us realize death isn't bad. Alas, I'm pretty sure death is horrifying and trying to lose the fear of it is just how some people cope with a calamity they can't do anything about.
